title: Abraham smashes the idols
summary: In Genesis Rabbah, Abraham smashes the idols in his father's shop, blames the largest one, and is thrown into a furnace by Nimrod. In the Quran, Abraham breaks the idols except the biggest, tells the people to ask them, and is thrown into a fire made cool.

title: The Buddha becomes a Christian saint
summary: The life of the Buddha passed through Manichaean and Arabic versions (Bilawhar wa-Būdhāsf) into the Georgian Balavariani and the Greek Barlaam and Ioasaph. Josaphat became a saint in the Christian calendar.

evidence.text: The name chain bodhisattva → Būdhāsaf → Yūdāsaf → Iōasaph is the lexical spine of the lead.

title: The raven that teaches burial
summary: In the Quran a raven shows Cain how to bury Abel. In Pirqei de-Rabbi Eliezer a raven shows Adam and Eve.

passages.text: فَبَعَثَ ٱللَّهُ غُرَابًا يَبْحَثُ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ لِيُرِيَهُۥ كَيْفَ يُوَٰرِى سَوْءَةَ أَخِيهِ قَالَ يَٰوَيْلَتَىٰٓ أَعَجَزْتُ أَنْ أَكُونَ مِثْلَ هَٰذَا ٱلْغُرَابِ فَأُوَٰرِىَ سَوْءَةَ أَخِى فَأَصْبَحَ مِنَ ٱلنَّٰدِمِينَ

evidence.text: Who learns from the raven differs (Cain vs. Adam). Dating PRE relative to the Quran is part of the question.

title: Jesus brings clay birds to life
summary: In the Infancy Gospel of Thomas the child Jesus shapes sparrows from clay and makes them fly. The Quran has Jesus fashion birds from clay that become birds by God's permission.

passages.text: (3:49) وَرَسُولًا إِلَىٰ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ أَنِّى قَدْ جِئْتُكُم بِـَٔايَةٍ مِّن رَّبِّكُمْ أَنِّىٓ أَخْلُقُ لَكُم مِّنَ ٱلطِّينِ كَهَيْـَٔةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ فَأَنفُخُ فِيهِ فَيَكُونُ طَيْرًۢا بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ وَأُبْرِئُ ٱلْأَكْمَهَ وَٱلْأَبْرَصَ وَأُحْىِ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ وَأُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا تَأْكُلُونَ وَمَا تَدَّخِرُونَ فِى بُيُوتِكُمْ إِنَّ فِى ذَٰلِكَ لَءَايَةً لَّكُمْ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ (5:110) إِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ يَٰعِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ ٱذْكُرْ نِعْمَتِى عَلَيْكَ وَعَلَىٰ وَٰلِدَتِكَ إِذْ أَيَّدتُّكَ بِرُوحِ ٱلْقُدُسِ تُكَلِّمُ ٱلنَّاسَ فِى ٱلْمَهْدِ وَكَهْلًا وَإِذْ عَلَّمْتُكَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَٱلْحِكْمَةَ وَٱلتَّوْرَىٰةَ وَٱلْإِنجِيلَ وَإِذْ تَخْلُقُ مِنَ ٱلطِّينِ كَهَيْـَٔةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ بِإِذْنِى فَتَنفُخُ فِيهَا فَتَكُونُ طَيْرًۢا بِإِذْنِى وَتُبْرِئُ ٱلْأَكْمَهَ وَٱلْأَبْرَصَ بِإِذْنِى وَإِذْ تُخْرِجُ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ بِإِذْنِى وَإِذْ كَفَفْتُ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ عَنكَ إِذْ جِئْتَهُم بِٱلْبَيِّنَٰتِ فَقَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ مِنْهُمْ إِنْ هَٰذَآ إِلَّا سِحْرٌ مُّبِينٌ

evidence.text: The Quran adds 'by God's permission' (bi-idhnī), which reframes the miracle theologically. That is a response-type detail.

title: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Alexander legends
summary: The Quran's Dhul-Qarnayn travels to where the sun sets and rises and builds a barrier against Gog and Magog. The Syriac Alexander Legend and the Alexander Romance have close parallels.

evidence.text: The Syriac Legend is often dated around 630 (Reinink), close to the Quran. The direction and the dating are both debated.

title: Flood narratives across traditions
summary: A divinely sent flood with a chosen survivor appears in Sumerian, Akkadian, Hebrew, Quranic, Vedic, Greek, and Chinese sources. The Near Eastern versions are historically linked; the others are candidate convergences.

passages.text_omitted: longer than 12 verses; read it in the source

passages.ref: Shujing; Mencius (Gun and Yu tame the flood)

evidence.text: Specificity test: the bird-release sequence (Gilgamesh XI; Genesis 8) is a rare motif combination that marks the Mesopotamian–Hebrew link. The Quran has no bird release.
Noah's drowned son (Quran 11:42–43) has no Genesis counterpart and is a sub-lead.
The Chinese story is about controlling the flood, not surviving it, so it is a weak match.

title: Han Kitab: Islam in Neo-Confucian terms
summary: Chinese Muslim scholars such as Wang Daiyu and Liu Zhi expressed tawḥīd with Neo-Confucian metaphysics: 真一 'the Real One', li and qi, and the Supreme Ultimate, in dialogue with Zhu Xi.

passages.ref: Zhu Xi, commentaries; Zhou Dunyi, Taijitu shuo

title: haykal: the Sumerian 'big house'
summary: Sumerian é-gal ('big house', palace) became Akkadian ekallu, Hebrew hêkhāl (palace, temple), Aramaic hêkhlā, and Arabic haykal.

evidence.text: haykal does not occur in the Quran; it is a control case for the lexical track.

title: ʼâçôwn: a word shared by Joseph and Moses
summary: אָסוֹן (ʼâçôwn, H611) occurs in 5 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Joseph (3) and Moses (2). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וְאֶת בִּנְיָמִין֙ אֲחִ֣י יוֹסֵ֔ף לֹא שָׁלַ֥ח יַעֲקֹ֖ב אֶת אֶחָ֑יו כִּ֣י אָמַ֔ר פֶּן יִקְרָאֶ֖נּוּ אָסֽוֹן
וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לֹֽא יֵרֵ֥ד בְּנִ֖י עִמָּכֶ֑ם כִּֽי אָחִ֨יו מֵ֜ת וְה֧וּא לְבַדּ֣וֹ נִשְׁאָ֗ר וּקְרָאָ֤הוּ אָסוֹן֙ בַּדֶּ֨רֶךְ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תֵּֽלְכוּ בָ֔הּ וְהוֹרַדְתֶּ֧ם אֶת שֵׂיבָתִ֛י בְּיָג֖וֹן שְׁאֽוֹלָה
וּלְקַחְתֶּ֧ם גַּם אֶת זֶ֛ה מֵעִ֥ם פָּנַ֖י וְקָרָ֣הוּ אָס֑וֹן וְהֽוֹרַדְתֶּ֧ם אֶת שֵׂיבָתִ֛י בְּרָעָ֖ה שְׁאֹֽלָה
וְכִֽי יִנָּצ֣וּ אֲנָשִׁ֗ים וְנָ֨גְפ֜וּ אִשָּׁ֤ה הָרָה֙ וְיָצְא֣וּ יְלָדֶ֔יהָ וְלֹ֥א יִהְיֶ֖ה אָס֑וֹן עָנ֣וֹשׁ יֵעָנֵ֗שׁ כַּֽאֲשֶׁ֨ר יָשִׁ֤ית עָלָיו֙ בַּ֣עַל הָֽאִשָּׁ֔ה וְנָתַ֖ן בִּפְלִלִֽים
וְאִם אָס֖וֹן יִהְיֶ֑ה וְנָתַתָּ֥ה נֶ֖פֶשׁ תַּ֥חַת נָֽפֶשׁ

title: bᵉkîyrâh: a word shared by Jacob and Saul
summary: בְּכִירָה (bᵉkîyrâh, H1067) occurs in 6 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Jacob (1) and Saul (1). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וַתֹּ֧אמֶר הַבְּכִירָ֛ה אֶל הַצְּעִירָ֖ה אָבִ֣ינוּ זָקֵ֑ן וְאִ֨ישׁ אֵ֤ין בָּאָ֨רֶץ֙ לָב֣וֹא עָלֵ֔ינוּ כְּדֶ֖רֶךְ כָּל הָאָֽרֶץ
וַתַּשְׁקֶ֧יןָ אֶת אֲבִיהֶ֛ן יַ֖יִן בַּלַּ֣יְלָה ה֑וּא וַתָּבֹ֤א הַבְּכִירָה֙ וַתִּשְׁכַּ֣ב אֶת אָבִ֔יהָ וְלֹֽא יָדַ֥ע בְּשִׁכְבָ֖הּ וּבְקׄוּמָֽהּ
וַֽיְהִי֙ מִֽמָּחֳרָ֔ת וַתֹּ֤אמֶר הַבְּכִירָה֙ אֶל הַצְּעִירָ֔ה הֵן שָׁכַ֥בְתִּי אֶ֖מֶשׁ אֶת אָבִ֑י נַשְׁקֶ֨נּוּ יַ֜יִן גַּם הַלַּ֗יְלָה וּבֹ֨אִי֙ שִׁכְבִ֣י עִמּ֔וֹ וּנְחַיֶּ֥ה מֵאָבִ֖ינוּ זָֽרַע
וַתֵּ֤לֶד הַבְּכִירָה֙ בֵּ֔ן וַתִּקְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖וֹ מוֹאָ֑ב ה֥וּא אֲבִֽי מוֹאָ֖ב עַד הַיּֽוֹם
וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָבָ֔ן לֹא יֵעָשֶׂ֥ה כֵ֖ן בִּמְקוֹמֵ֑נוּ לָתֵ֥ת הַצְּעִירָ֖ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַבְּכִירָֽה
וַיִּֽהְיוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י שָׁא֔וּל יוֹנָתָ֥ן וְיִשְׁוִ֖י וּמַלְכִּי שׁ֑וּעַ וְשֵׁם֙ שְׁתֵּ֣י בְנֹתָ֔יו שֵׁ֤ם הַבְּכִירָה֙ מֵרַ֔ב וְשֵׁ֥ם הַקְּטַנָּ֖ה מִיכַֽל

title: bᵉsôwrâh: a word shared by David and Elisha
summary: בְּשׂוֹרָה (bᵉsôwrâh, H1309) occurs in 6 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: David (5) and Elisha (1). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: כִּ֣י הַמַּגִּיד֩ לִ֨י לֵאמֹ֜ר הִנֵּה מֵ֣ת שָׁא֗וּל וְהֽוּא הָיָ֤ה כִמְבַשֵּׂר֙ בְּעֵינָ֔יו וָאֹחֲזָ֣ה ב֔וֹ וָאֶהְרְגֵ֖הוּ בְּצִֽקְלָ֑ג אֲשֶׁ֥ר לְתִתִּי ל֖וֹ בְּשֹׂרָֽה
וַיֹּ֧אמֶר ל֣וֹ יוֹאָ֗ב לֹא֩ אִ֨ישׁ בְּשֹׂרָ֤ה אַתָּה֙ הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה וּבִשַּׂרְתָּ֖ בְּי֣וֹם אַחֵ֑ר וְהַיּ֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ לֹ֣א תְבַשֵּׂ֔ר כִּֽי על עַל כֵּ֥ן בֶּן הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ מֵֽת

וַיֹּ֨סֶף ע֜וֹד אֲחִימַ֤עַץ בֶּן צָדוֹק֙ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֶל יוֹאָ֔ב וִ֣יהִי מָ֔ה אָרֻֽצָה נָּ֥א גַם אָ֖נִי אַחֲרֵ֣י הַכּוּשִׁ֑י וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יוֹאָ֗ב לָֽמָּה זֶּ֞ה אַתָּ֥ה רָץ֙ בְּנִ֔י וּלְכָ֖ה אֵין בְּשׂוֹרָ֥ה מֹצֵֽאת
וַיִּקְרָ֤א הַצֹּפֶה֙ וַיַּגֵּ֣ד לַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אִם לְבַדּ֖וֹ בְּשׂוֹרָ֣ה בְּפִ֑יו וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ הָל֖וֹךְ וְקָרֵֽב
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הַצֹּפֶ֔ה אֲנִ֤י רֹאֶה֙ אֶת מְרוּצַ֣ת הָרִאשׁ֔וֹן כִּמְרֻצַ֖ת אֲחִימַ֣עַץ בֶּן צָד֑וֹק וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אִֽישׁ ט֣וֹב זֶ֔ה וְאֶל בְּשׂוֹרָ֥ה טוֹבָ֖ה יָבֽוֹא

וַיֹּאמְרוּ֩ אִ֨ישׁ אֶל רֵעֵ֜הוּ לֹֽא כֵ֣ן אֲנַ֣חְנוּ עֹשִׂ֗ים הַיּ֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ יוֹם בְּשֹׂרָ֣ה ה֔וּא וַאֲנַ֣חְנוּ מַחְשִׁ֗ים וְחִכִּ֛ינוּ עַד א֥וֹר הַבֹּ֖קֶר וּמְצָאָ֣נוּ עָו֑וֹן וְעַתָּה֙ לְכ֣וּ וְנָבֹ֔אָה וְנַגִּ֖ידָה בֵּ֥ית הַמֶּֽלֶךְ

title: dâth: a word shared by Esther and Moses
summary: דָּת (dâth, H1881) occurs in 21 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Esther (19) and Moses (1). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וַיֹּאמַ֗ר יְהוָ֞ה מִסִּינַ֥י בָּא֙ וְזָרַ֤ח מִשֵּׂעִיר֙ לָ֔מוֹ הוֹפִ֨יעַ֙ מֵהַ֣ר פָּארָ֔ן וְאָתָ֖ה מֵרִבְבֹ֣ת קֹ֑דֶשׁ מִֽימִינ֕וֹ אשדת אֵ֥שׁ דָּ֖ת לָֽמוֹ
וַֽיִּתְּנ֣וּ אֶת דָּתֵ֣י הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ לַאֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנֵי֙ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וּפַחֲו֖וֹת עֵ֣בֶר הַנָּהָ֑ר וְנִשְּׂא֥וּ אֶת הָעָ֖ם וְאֶת בֵּֽית הָאֱלֹהִֽים
וְהַשְּׁתִיָּ֥ה כַדָּ֖ת אֵ֣ין אֹנֵ֑ס כִּי כֵ֣ן יִסַּ֣ד הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ עַ֚ל כָּל רַ֣ב בֵּית֔וֹ לַעֲשׂ֖וֹת כִּרְצ֥וֹן אִישׁ וָאִֽישׁ
וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לַחֲכָמִ֖ים יֹדְעֵ֣י הָֽעִתִּ֑ים כִּי כֵן֙ דְּבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לִפְנֵ֕י כָּל יֹדְעֵ֖י דָּ֥ת וָדִֽין
כְּדָת֙ מַֽה לַּעֲשׂ֔וֹת בַּמַּלְכָּ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֑י עַ֣ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא עָשְׂתָ֗ה אֶֽת מַאֲמַר֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ בְּיַ֖ד הַסָּרִיסִֽים

אִם עַל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֗וֹב יֵצֵ֤א דְבַר מַלְכוּת֙ מִלְּפָנָ֔יו וְיִכָּתֵ֛ב בְּדָתֵ֥י פָֽרַס וּמָדַ֖י וְלֹ֣א יַעֲב֑וֹר אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹֽא תָב֜וֹא וַשְׁתִּ֗י לִפְנֵי֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ וּמַלְכוּתָהּ֙ יִתֵּ֣ן הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לִרְעוּתָ֖הּ הַטּוֹבָ֥ה מִמֶּֽנָּה

וַיְהִ֗י בְּהִשָּׁמַ֤ע דְּבַר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְדָת֔וֹ וּֽבְהִקָּבֵ֞ץ נְעָר֥וֹת רַבּ֛וֹת אֶל שׁוּשַׁ֥ן הַבִּירָ֖ה אֶל יַ֣ד הֵגָ֑י וַתִּלָּקַ֤ח אֶסְתֵּר֙ אֶל בֵּ֣ית הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֶל יַ֥ד הֵגַ֖י שֹׁמֵ֥ר הַנָּשִֽׁים

וּבְהַגִּ֡יעַ תֹּר֩ נַעֲרָ֨ה וְנַעֲרָ֜ה לָב֣וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֗וֹשׁ מִקֵּץ֩ הֱי֨וֹת לָ֜הּ כְּדָ֤ת הַנָּשִׁים֙ שְׁנֵ֣ים עָשָׂ֣ר חֹ֔דֶשׁ כִּ֛י כֵּ֥ן יִמְלְא֖וּ יְמֵ֣י מְרוּקֵיהֶ֑ן שִׁשָּׁ֤ה חֳדָשִׁים֙ בְּשֶׁ֣מֶן הַמֹּ֔ר וְשִׁשָּׁ֤ה חֳדָשִׁים֙ בַּבְּשָׂמִ֔ים וּבְתַמְרוּקֵ֖י הַנָּשִֽׁים

וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הָמָן֙ לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ יֶשְׁנ֣וֹ עַם אֶחָ֗ד מְפֻזָּ֤ר וּמְפֹרָד֙ בֵּ֣ין הָֽעַמִּ֔ים בְּכֹ֖ל מְדִינ֣וֹת מַלְכוּתֶ֑ךָ וְדָתֵיהֶ֞ם שֹׁנ֣וֹת מִכָּל עָ֗ם וְאֶת דָּתֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֵינָ֣ם עֹשִׂ֔ים וְלַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֵין שֹׁוֶ֖ה לְהַנִּיחָֽם
פַּתְשֶׁ֣גֶן הַכְּתָ֗ב לְהִנָּ֤תֵֽן דָּת֙ בְּכָל מְדִינָ֣ה וּמְדִינָ֔ה גָּל֖וּי לְכָל הָֽעַמִּ֑ים לִהְי֥וֹת עֲתִדִ֖ים לַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה
הָֽרָצִ֞ים יָצְא֤וּ דְחוּפִים֙ בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְהַדָּ֥ת נִתְּנָ֖ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֑ה וְהַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְהָמָן֙ יָשְׁב֣וּ לִשְׁתּ֔וֹת וְהָעִ֥יר שׁוּשָׁ֖ן נָבֽוֹכָה
וּבְכָל מְדִינָ֣ה וּמְדִינָ֗ה מְקוֹם֙ אֲשֶׁ֨ר דְּבַר הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְדָתוֹ֙ מַגִּ֔יעַ אֵ֤בֶל גָּדוֹל֙ לַיְּהוּדִ֔ים וְצ֥וֹם וּבְכִ֖י וּמִסְפֵּ֑ד שַׂ֣ק וָאֵ֔פֶר יֻצַּ֖ע לָֽרַבִּֽים

וְאֶת פַּתְשֶׁ֣גֶן כְּתָֽב הַ֠דָּת אֲשֶׁר נִתַּ֨ן בְּשׁוּשָׁ֤ן לְהַשְׁמִידָם֙ נָ֣תַן ל֔וֹ לְהַרְא֥וֹת אֶת אֶסְתֵּ֖ר וּלְהַגִּ֣יד לָ֑הּ וּלְצַוּ֣וֹת עָלֶ֗יהָ לָב֨וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֧לֶךְ לְהִֽתְחַנֶּן ל֛וֹ וּלְבַקֵּ֥שׁ מִלְּפָנָ֖יו עַל עַמָּֽהּ

כָּל עַבְדֵ֣י הַמֶּ֡לֶךְ וְעַם מְדִינ֨וֹת הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ יֽוֹדְעִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר כָּל אִ֣ישׁ וְאִשָּׁ֡ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר יָבֽוֹא אֶל הַמֶּלֶךְ֩ אֶל הֶחָצֵ֨ר הַפְּנִימִ֜ית אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא יִקָּרֵ֗א אַחַ֤ת דָּתוֹ֙ לְהָמִ֔ית לְ֠בַד מֵאֲשֶׁ֨ר יֽוֹשִׁיט ל֥וֹ הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ אֶת שַׁרְבִ֥יט הַזָּהָ֖ב וְחָיָ֑ה וַאֲנִ֗י לֹ֤א נִקְרֵ֨אתי֙ לָב֣וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ זֶ֖ה שְׁלוֹשִׁ֥ים יֽוֹם

לֵךְ֩ כְּנ֨וֹס אֶת כָּל הַיְּהוּדִ֜ים הַֽנִּמְצְאִ֣ים בְּשׁוּשָׁ֗ן וְצ֣וּמוּ עָ֠לַי וְאַל תֹּאכְל֨וּ וְאַל תִּשְׁתּ֜וּ שְׁלֹ֤שֶׁת יָמִים֙ לַ֣יְלָה וָי֔וֹם גַּם אֲנִ֥י וְנַעֲרֹתַ֖י אָצ֣וּם כֵּ֑ן וּבְכֵ֞ן אָב֤וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא כַדָּ֔ת וְכַאֲשֶׁ֥ר אָבַ֖דְתִּי אָבָֽדְתִּי

title: malkâh: a word shared by Esther and Solomon
summary: מַלְכָּה (malkâh, H4436) occurs in 34 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Esther (24) and Solomon (8). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וּמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א שֹׁמַ֛עַת אֶת שֵׁ֥מַע שְׁלֹמֹ֖ה לְשֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה וַתָּבֹ֥א לְנַסֹּת֖וֹ בְּחִידֽוֹת
וַתֵּ֨רֶא֙ מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֔א אֵ֖ת כָּל חָכְמַ֣ת שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וְהַבַּ֖יִת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנָֽה

וַתִּתֵּ֨ן לַמֶּ֜לֶךְ מֵאָ֥ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֣ים כִּכַּ֣ר זָהָ֗ב וּבְשָׂמִ֛ים הַרְבֵּ֥ה מְאֹ֖ד וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה לֹא בָא֩ כַבֹּ֨שֶׂם הַה֥וּא עוֹד֙ לָרֹ֔ב אֲשֶׁר נָתְנָ֥ה מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֖א לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹֽה
וְהַמֶּ֨לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֜ה נָתַ֣ן לְמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א אֶת כָּל חֶפְצָהּ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁאָ֔לָה מִלְּבַד֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָֽתַן לָ֔הּ כְּיַ֖ד הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וַתֵּ֛פֶן וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ לְאַרְצָ֖הּ הִ֥יא וַעֲבָדֶֽיהָ

וּמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א שָֽׁמְעָה֮ אֶת שֵׁ֣מַע שְׁלֹמֹה֒ וַתָּב֣וֹא לְנַסּוֹת֩ אֶת שְׁלֹמֹ֨ה בְחִיד֜וֹת בִּירֽוּשָׁלִַ֗ם בְּחַ֣יִל כָּבֵ֣ד מְאֹ֡ד וּ֠גְמַלִּים נֹשְׂאִ֨ים בְּשָׂמִ֧ים וְזָהָ֛ב לָרֹ֖ב וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה וַתָּבוֹא֙ אֶל שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה וַתְּדַבֵּ֣ר עִמּ֔וֹ אֵ֛ת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָיָ֖ה עִם לְבָבָֽהּ
וַתֵּ֨רֶא֙ מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֔א אֵ֖ת חָכְמַ֣ת שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וְהַבַּ֖יִת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנָֽה
וַתִּתֵּ֨ן לַמֶּ֜לֶךְ מֵאָ֥ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֣ים כִּכַּ֣ר זָהָ֗ב וּבְשָׂמִ֛ים לָרֹ֥ב מְאֹ֖ד וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה וְלֹ֤א הָיָה֙ כַּבֹּ֣שֶׂם הַה֔וּא אֲשֶׁר נָתְנָ֥ה מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֖א לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹֽה
וְהַמֶּ֨לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֜ה נָתַ֣ן לְמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א אֶת כָּל חֶפְצָהּ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁאָ֔לָה מִלְּבַ֖ד אֲשֶׁר הֵבִ֣יאָה אֶל הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַֽתַּהֲפֹ֛ךְ וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ לְאַרְצָ֖הּ הִ֥יא וַעֲבָדֶֽיהָ
גַּ֚ם וַשְׁתִּ֣י הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה עָשְׂתָ֖ה מִשְׁתֵּ֣ה נָשִׁ֑ים בֵּ֚ית הַמַּלְכ֔וּת אֲשֶׁ֖ר לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֽוֹשׁ
לְ֠הָבִיא אֶת וַשְׁתִּ֧י הַמַּלְכָּ֛ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ בְּכֶ֣תֶר מַלְכ֑וּת לְהַרְא֨וֹת הָֽעַמִּ֤ים וְהַשָּׂרִים֙ אֶת יָפְיָ֔הּ כִּֽי טוֹבַ֥ת מַרְאֶ֖ה הִֽיא
וַתְּמָאֵ֞ן הַמַּלְכָּ֣ה וַשְׁתִּ֗י לָבוֹא֙ בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּיַ֣ד הַסָּרִיסִ֑ים וַיִּקְצֹ֤ף הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ מְאֹ֔ד וַחֲמָת֖וֹ בָּעֲרָ֥ה בֽוֹ
כְּדָת֙ מַֽה לַּעֲשׂ֔וֹת בַּמַּלְכָּ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֑י עַ֣ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא עָשְׂתָ֗ה אֶֽת מַאֲמַר֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ בְּיַ֖ד הַסָּרִיסִֽים

וַיֹּ֣אמֶר מומכן מְמוּכָ֗ן לִפְנֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְהַשָּׂרִ֔ים לֹ֤א עַל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ לְבַדּ֔וֹ עָוְתָ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֣י הַמַּלְכָּ֑ה כִּ֤י עַל כָּל הַשָּׂרִים֙ וְעַל כָּל הָ֣עַמִּ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֕ר בְּכָל מְדִינ֖וֹת הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֽוֹשׁ
כִּֽי יֵצֵ֤א דְבַר הַמַּלְכָּה֙ עַל כָּל הַנָּשִׁ֔ים לְהַבְז֥וֹת בַּעְלֵיהֶ֖ן בְּעֵינֵיהֶ֑ן בְּאָמְרָ֗ם הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֡וֹשׁ אָמַ֞ר לְהָבִ֨יא אֶת וַשְׁתִּ֧י הַמַּלְכָּ֛ה לְפָנָ֖יו וְלֹא בָֽאָה
וְֽהַיּ֨וֹם הַזֶּ֜ה תֹּאמַ֣רְנָה שָׂר֣וֹת פָּֽרַס וּמָדַ֗י אֲשֶׁ֤ר שָֽׁמְעוּ֙ אֶת דְּבַ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה לְכֹ֖ל שָׂרֵ֣י הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וּכְדַ֖י בִּזָּי֥וֹן וָקָֽצֶף

summary: מִלָּה (millâh, H4405) occurs in 38 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: David (1) and Job (34). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: ר֥וּחַ יְהוָ֖ה דִּבֶּר בִּ֑י וּמִלָּת֖וֹ עַל לְשׁוֹנִֽי
הֲנִסָּ֬ה דָבָ֣ר אֵלֶ֣יךָ תִּלְאֶ֑ה וַעְצֹ֥ר בְּ֝מִלִּ֗ין מִ֣י יוּכָֽל
כּ֭וֹשֵׁל יְקִימ֣וּן מִלֶּ֑יךָ וּבִרְכַּ֖יִם כֹּרְע֣וֹת תְּאַמֵּֽץ
הַלְהוֹכַ֣ח מִלִּ֣ים תַּחְשֹׁ֑בוּ וּ֝לְר֗וּחַ אִמְרֵ֥י נֹאָֽשׁ
הֲלֹא הֵ֣ם י֭וֹרוּךָ יֹ֣אמְרוּ לָ֑ךְ וּ֝מִלִּבָּ֗ם יוֹצִ֥אוּ מִלִּֽים
הֲלֹא אֹ֭זֶן מִלִּ֣ין תִּבְחָ֑ן וְ֝חֵ֗ךְ אֹ֣כֶל יִטְעַם לֽוֹ
שִׁמְע֣וּ שָׁ֭מוֹעַ מִלָּתִ֑י וְ֝אַֽחֲוָתִ֗י בְּאָזְנֵיכֶֽם
הוֹכֵ֣חַ בְּ֭דָבָר לֹ֣א יִסְכּ֑וֹן וּ֝מִלִּ֗ים לֹא יוֹעִ֥יל בָּֽם

וַיַּ֥רְא שַׂר הָאֹפִ֖ים כִּ֣י ט֣וֹב פָּתָ֑ר וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל יוֹסֵ֔ף אַף אֲנִי֙ בַּחֲלוֹמִ֔י וְהִנֵּ֗ה שְׁלֹשָׁ֛ה סַלֵּ֥י חֹרִ֖י עַל רֹאשִֽׁי
וְאֵ֛ת שַׂ֥ר הָאֹפִ֖ים תָּלָ֑ה כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר פָּתַ֛ר לָהֶ֖ם יוֹסֵֽף
וַיְהִ֤י בַבֹּ֨קֶר֙ וַתִּפָּ֣עֶם רוּח֔וֹ וַיִּשְׁלַ֗ח וַיִּקְרָ֛א אֶת כָּל חַרְטֻמֵּ֥י מִצְרַ֖יִם וְאֶת כָּל חֲכָמֶ֑יהָ וַיְסַפֵּ֨ר פַּרְעֹ֤ה לָהֶם֙ אֶת חֲלֹמ֔וֹ וְאֵין פּוֹתֵ֥ר אוֹתָ֖ם לְפַרְעֹֽה
וְשָׁ֨ם אִתָּ֜נוּ נַ֣עַר עִבְרִ֗י עֶ֚בֶד לְשַׂ֣ר הַטַּבָּחִ֔ים וַנְּ֨סַפֶּר ל֔וֹ וַיִּפְתָּר לָ֖נוּ אֶת חֲלֹמֹתֵ֑ינוּ אִ֥ישׁ כַּחֲלֹמ֖וֹ פָּתָֽר
וַיְהִ֛י כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר פָּֽתַר לָ֖נוּ כֵּ֣ן הָיָ֑ה אֹתִ֛י הֵשִׁ֥יב עַל כַּנִּ֖י וְאֹת֥וֹ תָלָֽה
וַיֹּ֤אמֶר פַּרְעֹה֙ אֶל יוֹסֵ֔ף חֲל֣וֹם חָלַ֔מְתִּי וּפֹתֵ֖ר אֵ֣ין אֹת֑וֹ וַאֲנִ֗י שָׁמַ֤עְתִּי עָלֶ֨יךָ֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר תִּשְׁמַ֥ע חֲל֖וֹם לִפְתֹּ֥ר אֹתֽוֹ

passages.text: אֶת הַמְּנֹרָ֨ה הַטְּהֹרָ֜ה אֶת נֵרֹתֶ֗יהָ נֵרֹ֛ת הַמַּֽעֲרָכָ֖ה וְאֶת כָּל כֵּלֶ֑יהָ וְאֵ֖ת שֶׁ֥מֶן הַמָּאֽוֹר
וְשַׂמְתָּ֥ אוֹתָ֛ם שְׁתַּ֥יִם מַֽעֲרָכ֖וֹת שֵׁ֣שׁ הַֽמַּעֲרָ֑כֶת עַ֛ל הַשֻּׁלְחָ֥ן הַטָּהֹ֖ר לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה
וּבָנִ֨יתָ מִזְבֵּ֜חַ לַיהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֗יךָ עַ֣ל רֹ֧אשׁ הַמָּע֛וֹז הַזֶּ֖ה בַּמַּֽעֲרָכָ֑ה וְלָֽקַחְתָּ֙ אֶת הַפָּ֣ר הַשֵּׁנִ֔י וְהַעֲלִ֣יתָ עוֹלָ֔ה בַּעֲצֵ֥י הָאֲשֵׁרָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר תִּכְרֹֽת
וַיַּעַרְכ֨וּ פְלִשְׁתִּ֜ים לִקְרַ֣את יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל וַתִּטֹּשׁ֙ הַמִּלְחָמָ֔ה וַיִּנָּ֥גֶף יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לִפְנֵ֣י פְלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וַיַּכּ֤וּ בַמַּֽעֲרָכָה֙ בַּשָּׂדֶ֔ה כְּאַרְבַּ֥עַת אֲלָפִ֖ים אִֽישׁ
וַיָּ֤רָץ אִישׁ בִּנְיָמִן֙ מֵהַמַּ֣עֲרָכָ֔ה וַיָּבֹ֥א שִׁלֹ֖ה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא וּמַדָּ֣יו קְרֻעִ֔ים וַאֲדָמָ֖ה עַל רֹאשֽׁוֹ
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הָאִ֜ישׁ אֶל עֵלִ֗י אָֽנֹכִי֙ הַבָּ֣א מִן הַמַּעֲרָכָ֔ה וַאֲנִ֕י מִן הַמַּעֲרָכָ֖ה נַ֣סְתִּי הַיּ֑וֹם וַיֹּ֛אמֶר מֶֽה הָיָ֥ה הַדָּבָ֖ר בְּנִֽי

וַֽיַּעֲמֹ֗ד וַיִּקְרָא֙ אֶל מַעַרְכֹ֣ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהֶ֔ם לָ֥מָּה תֵצְא֖וּ לַעֲרֹ֣ךְ מִלְחָמָ֑ה הֲל֧וֹא אָנֹכִ֣י הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֗י וְאַתֶּם֙ עֲבָדִ֣ים לְשָׁא֔וּל בְּרוּ לָכֶ֥ם אִ֖ישׁ וְיֵרֵ֥ד אֵלָֽי
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔י אֲנִ֗י חֵרַ֛פְתִּי אֶת מַעַרְכ֥וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה תְּנוּ לִ֣י אִ֔ישׁ וְנִֽלָּחֲמָ֖ה יָֽחַד

וַיַּשְׁכֵּ֨ם דָּוִ֜ד בַּבֹּ֗קֶר וַיִּטֹּ֤שׁ אֶת הַצֹּאן֙ עַל שֹׁמֵ֔ר וַיִּשָּׂ֣א וַיֵּ֔לֶךְ כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר צִוָּ֖הוּ יִשָׁ֑י וַיָּבֹא֙ הַמַּעְגָּ֔לָה וְהַחַ֗יִל הַיֹּצֵא֙ אֶל הַמַּ֣עֲרָכָ֔ה וְהֵרֵ֖עוּ בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה
וַתַּעֲרֹ֤ךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ וּפְלִשְׁתִּ֔ים מַעֲרָכָ֖ה לִקְרַ֥את מַעֲרָכָֽה
וַיִּטֹּשׁ֩ דָּוִ֨ד אֶת הַכֵּלִ֜ים מֵעָלָ֗יו עַל יַד֙ שׁוֹמֵ֣ר הַכֵּלִ֔ים וַיָּ֖רָץ הַמַּעֲרָכָ֑ה וַיָּבֹ֕א וַיִּשְׁאַ֥ל לְאֶחָ֖יו לְשָׁלֽוֹם
וְה֣וּא מְדַבֵּ֣ר עִמָּ֗ם וְהִנֵּ֣ה אִ֣ישׁ הַבֵּנַ֡יִם עוֹלֶ֞ה גָּלְיָת֩ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֨י שְׁמ֤וֹ מִגַּת֙ ממערות מִמַּעַרְכ֣וֹת פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וַיְדַבֵּ֖ר כַּדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וַיִּשְׁמַ֖ע דָּוִֽד

וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֗ד אֶֽל הָאֲנָשִׁ֞ים הָעֹמְדִ֣ים עִמּוֹ֮ לֵאמֹר֒ מַה יֵּעָשֶׂ֗ה לָאִישׁ֙ אֲשֶׁ֤ר יַכֶּה֙ אֶת הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֣י הַלָּ֔ז וְהֵסִ֥יר חֶרְפָּ֖ה מֵעַ֣ל יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כִּ֣י מִ֗י הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֤י הֶֽעָרֵל֙ הַזֶּ֔ה כִּ֣י חֵרֵ֔ף מַעַרְכ֖וֹת אֱלֹהִ֥ים חַיִּֽים
גַּ֧ם אֶֽת הָאֲרִ֛י גַּם הַדּ֖וֹב הִכָּ֣ה עַבְדֶּ֑ךָ וְֽ֠הָיָה הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֨י הֶעָרֵ֤ל הַזֶּה֙ כְּאַחַ֣ד מֵהֶ֔ם כִּ֣י חֵרֵ֔ף מַעַרְכֹ֖ת אֱלֹהִ֥ים חַיִּֽים
וַיֹּ֤אמֶר דָּוִד֙ אֶל הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔י אַתָּה֙ בָּ֣א אֵלַ֔י בְּחֶ֖רֶב וּבַחֲנִ֣ית וּבְכִיד֑וֹן וְאָנֹכִ֣י בָֽא אֵלֶ֗יךָ בְּשֵׁם֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֛י מַעַרְכ֥וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר חֵרַֽפְתָּ

title: Satan refuses to bow to Adam
summary: God commands the angels to honor Adam, and Satan refuses. Found in the Life of Adam and Eve and the Cave of Treasures, and repeatedly in the Quran.

passages.ref: Life of Adam and Eve (Latin Vita 12–16)

title: The Kalam cosmological argument
summary: The argument that the universe began and so has a cause, developed by the mutakallimūn and al-Ghazali, was revived and named by William Lane Craig in analytic philosophy of religion.

passages.ref: W. L. Craig, The Kalām Cosmological Argument (1979)

title: Panchatantra to Kalila wa-Dimna
summary: The Sanskrit Panchatantra was translated into Middle Persian (Burzoy, 6th c.), then Arabic (Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, 8th c.), then into Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and most European languages.

title: Kumarbi cycle and Hesiod's Theogony
summary: Both have the same succession myth: Anu, Kumarbi, Teshub in the Hurro-Hittite cycle and Ouranos, Kronos, Zeus in Hesiod, including a sky god castrated by his successor.

title: kursī: Sumerian throne to Quranic seat
summary: Sumerian guza passed into Akkadian kussû, Aramaic kursēʾ, and Arabic kursī. The Quran's Throne Verse (2:255) uses it.

passages.note: His kursī encompasses the heavens and the earth
passages.text: ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْحَىُّ ٱلْقَيُّومُ لَا تَأْخُذُهُۥ سِنَةٌ وَلَا نَوْمٌ لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ مَن ذَا ٱلَّذِى يَشْفَعُ عِندَهُۥٓ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِۦ يَعْلَمُ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَمَا خَلْفَهُمْ وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَىْءٍ مِّنْ عِلْمِهِۦٓ إِلَّا بِمَا شَآءَ وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ وَلَا يَـُٔودُهُۥ حِفْظُهُمَا وَهُوَ ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْعَظِيمُ
وَلَقَدْ فَتَنَّا سُلَيْمَٰنَ وَأَلْقَيْنَا عَلَىٰ كُرْسِيِّهِۦ جَسَدًا ثُمَّ أَنَابَ

evidence.text: Arabic kursī shows the Aramaic -r- form (dissimilated -ss- > -rs-), which points to Aramaic as the immediate source.

title: Mani and the 'seal of the prophets'
summary: Quran 33:40 calls Muhammad khātam al-nabiyyīn. Manichaean sources present Mani as the last in a line of prophets (Buddha, Zoroaster, Jesus), and whether 'seal' was a Manichaean title is debated.

passages.text: مَّا كَانَ مُحَمَّدٌ أَبَآ أَحَدٍ مِّن رِّجَالِكُمْ وَلَٰكِن رَّسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَخَاتَمَ ٱلنَّبِيِّۦنَ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ عَلِيمًا

title: Mary raised in the Temple
summary: The Protevangelium of James has Mary dedicated to the Temple, fed by an angel, and her guardian chosen by a sign. The Quran has Mary's dedication, miraculous provision in the sanctuary, Zechariah as guardian, and lots cast for her care.

passages.text: (3:35) إِذْ قَالَتِ ٱمْرَأَتُ عِمْرَٰنَ رَبِّ إِنِّى نَذَرْتُ لَكَ مَا فِى بَطْنِى مُحَرَّرًا فَتَقَبَّلْ مِنِّىٓ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ (3:36) فَلَمَّا وَضَعَتْهَا قَالَتْ رَبِّ إِنِّى وَضَعْتُهَآ أُنثَىٰ وَٱللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا وَضَعَتْ وَلَيْسَ ٱلذَّكَرُ كَٱلْأُنثَىٰ وَإِنِّى سَمَّيْتُهَا مَرْيَمَ وَإِنِّىٓ أُعِيذُهَا بِكَ وَذُرِّيَّتَهَا مِنَ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنِ ٱلرَّجِيمِ (3:37) فَتَقَبَّلَهَا رَبُّهَا بِقَبُولٍ حَسَنٍ وَأَنۢبَتَهَا نَبَاتًا حَسَنًا وَكَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّا كُلَّمَا دَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا زَكَرِيَّا ٱلْمِحْرَابَ وَجَدَ عِندَهَا رِزْقًا قَالَ يَٰمَرْيَمُ أَنَّىٰ لَكِ هَٰذَا قَالَتْ هُوَ مِنْ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشَآءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ (3:44) ذَٰلِكَ مِنْ أَنۢبَآءِ ٱلْغَيْبِ نُوحِيهِ إِلَيْكَ وَمَا كُنتَ لَدَيْهِمْ إِذْ يُلْقُونَ أَقْلَٰمَهُمْ أَيُّهُمْ يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ وَمَا كُنتَ لَدَيْهِمْ إِذْ يَخْتَصِمُونَ

title: Mary and the palm tree
summary: In Pseudo-Matthew a palm bends to feed Mary and a spring opens during the flight to Egypt. In the Quran a palm and a stream sustain Mary during the birth of Jesus.

Only in Solomon's gold, ivory throne, fleet and horse trade: Gold coming to the king each year weighs 666 talents; King makes hundreds of shields of beaten gold and hangs them in the palace; King's merchants import horses from Egypt and Kue and export chariots to Hittite and Aramean kings at fixed prices; Great ivory throne overlaid with gold, with six steps and twelve lions on the steps and two beside the arms; Tarshish ships every three years bring gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks (or baboons); The king makes silver and gold as common as stones and cedar as sycamores; Kings of all the earth send to hear the wise king's wisdom.

title: Solomon's foreign wives and apostasy ↔ Solomon, the devils and Harut and Marut

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/01-hb-quran.yaml).

title: The wounded prophet's parable against Ahab ↔ The ratio of the steadfast, captives and ransom
summary: 1 correspondence read side by side: 1 shared wording.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/03-hb-quran.yaml).

Shared motifs, rarest first: A prophet should not take captives until he has thoroughly subdued the land (weight 6.7); Conqueror spares the enemy king and best livestock against God's command (weight 6.0). Pair score 12.7.

Only in The wounded prophet's parable against Ahab: Wounded prophet, disguised with a bandage over his eyes, tells the king a case and the king condemns himself; Man who refuses a prophet's command to strike him is killed by a lion; 'Your life for his life': a guard who loses a prisoner forfeits his life or a talent of silver; King goes home 'sullen and angry' (sar ve-za'ef) after a prophet's rebuke; Band of prophets with harp, drum, flute and lyre prophesying in ecstasy; Ban (herem): total destruction of a conquered population.

Only in The ratio of the steadfast, captives and ransom: Captives with good in their hearts are promised better than what was taken from them; Twenty steadfast defeat two hundred, a hundred a thousand; later eased to one against two; Only a prior decree from God averted punishment for taking ransom; Blessing: five of you will chase a hundred, a hundred ten thousand; A ratio of the few who defeat (or are routed by) the many [divergence between the texts]; Livestock and spoil taken as booty after the ban; One chases a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight.

title: Naboth's vineyard ↔ The people of the town, the three messengers and the man who came running
summary: 1 correspondence read side by side: 1 shared wording.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/06-hb-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: Offender stoned to death by the community (weight 5.8). Pair score 5.8.

Only in Naboth's vineyard: Commoner refuses to sell or trade his ancestral vineyard to the king: 'God forbid I give you my fathers' inheritance'; Thwarted king lies on his bed, turns his face to the wall and refuses to eat; Queen writes letters in the king's name, sealed with his seal, ordering a judicial murder; A fast is proclaimed and two worthless men falsely testify that the victim 'blessed (cursed) God and king'; Innocent victim is taken outside the city and stoned to death; King goes home 'sullen and angry' (sar ve-za'ef) after a prophet's rebuke; Prohibition of coveting the neighbor's wife and property; Prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft and false witness.

title: Micaiah son of Imlah and the lying spirit ↔ Micaiah ben Imlah, the lying spirit in the divine council, and Ahab's death
summary: 7 shared motifs, found by the separate reads; not yet compared side by side.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Prophet first sarcastically repeats the favorable oracle, then under oath tells the true one (weight 6.7); A spirit volunteers in the divine council to be a lying spirit in the prophets' mouths (weight 6.7); A false prophet strikes the true prophet on the cheek (weight 6.7); Court prophet makes iron horns: 'with these you will gore Aram' (weight 6.7); Four hundred court prophets unanimously promise victory (weight 6.7); A single true prophet, hated by the king because he never prophesies good for him (weight 6.7); Prayer that the people not be 'like sheep without a shepherd' (weight 5.6). Pair score 45.7.

Only in Micaiah son of Imlah and the lying spirit: God asks the heavenly council 'who will entice the king?'; a spirit volunteers; Prophet imprisoned on short rations of bread and water until the king returns in peace; Prophet stakes his authority: 'If you return in peace, YHWH has not spoken by me'; Where false words in a prophet's message come from, and what becomes of them [divergence between the texts]; Prophet sees God seated on his throne with all the host of heaven standing to his right and left; Whether the adversary, devils or deceiving spirits have access to God's council [contrast between the texts]; God uses a false prophet to test whether Israel loves him.

Only in Micaiah ben Imlah, the lying spirit in the divine council, and Ahab's death: The enemy commander orders his chariots to fight no one but the king; When the threatened king cries out, God turns the attackers away from him; 'Hear, all you peoples' (quotation linking the prophet to Micah); One king entices (hesit) another into a disastrous war; Two kings sit in royal robes on thrones at the threshing floor by the city gate; A righteous king allies by marriage with a wicked king's house; Prophet imprisoned on 'bread of affliction and water of affliction'; The prophet swears to speak only what his God tells him; The wounded king props himself in his chariot all day and dies at sunset; An arrow shot at random strikes the king between the joints of his armor; A king disguises himself in battle while his ally wears royal robes; God enthroned with the host of heaven standing at his right and left deliberates.

Only in Micaiah son of Imlah and the lying spirit: God asks the heavenly council 'who will entice the king?'; a spirit volunteers; Prophet imprisoned on short rations of bread and water until the king returns in peace; Four hundred court prophets unanimously promise victory; Prophet stakes his authority: 'If you return in peace, YHWH has not spoken by me'; Court prophet makes iron horns: 'with these you will gore Aram'; A spirit volunteers in the divine council to be a lying spirit in the prophets' mouths; A single true prophet, hated by the king because he never prophesies good for him; Prophet first sarcastically repeats the favorable oracle, then under oath tells the true one; A false prophet strikes the true prophet on the cheek; Prophet sees God seated on his throne with all the host of heaven standing to his right and left; Whether the adversary, devils or deceiving spirits have access to God's council [contrast between the texts]; God uses a false prophet to test whether Israel loves him; and 1 more.

Only in Rejected prophets, ruined towns, the thousand-year day and Satan's insertion: Destroyed towns lie fallen on their roofs, with an abandoned well and a lofty palace; It is not the eyes that are blind but the hearts within the breasts; Satan casts something into every prophet's recitation or wish; God abrogates it and confirms his verses; Where false words in a prophet's message come from, and what becomes of them [contrast between the texts]; YHWH will be king over all the earth; in that day YHWH will be one and his name one; A thousand years in God's sight are like yesterday when it passes, or a watch in the night; Scoffers ask the prophet to hasten the punishment; it is held back only by an appointed term and will come suddenly; The listeners walk among the dwellings of generations God destroyed, a sign; A foolish people who have eyes but do not see and ears but do not hear; The Day of YHWH: a coming day of divine judgment, terror and darkness; Destruction follows the people's rejection of a messenger.

Only in The bronze sea, wheeled stands and temple vessels: Ten golden lampstands stand before the inner sanctuary, five on each side; Ten wheeled bronze stands decorated with lions, oxen, cherubim and palms carry basins; The bronze used for the sanctuary is so abundant its weight was not determined; Bronze vessels cast in the clay ground of the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zarethan; A round vessel ten cubits across measures thirty around (pi taken as three); Exact dimensions in cubits are given for a sacred object of the sanctuary; An accounting of the gold, silver and bronze used for the sanctuary; A bronze laver where priests wash hands and feet before service, lest they die; A small gold-plated altar for burning incense before the veil; A gold table with the bread of the presence always before God.

title: Hiram the bronze-smith and the pillars Jachin and Boaz ↔ David's mountains and mail; Solomon's wind, copper, jinn and staff
summary: 1 correspondence read side by side: 1 deliberately changed.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/06-hb-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: Who did Solomon's building and craft work [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.3). Pair score 6.3.

Only in Hiram the bronze-smith and the pillars Jachin and Boaz: Master bronze-smith is son of an Israelite widow and a Tyrian father, filled with wisdom and skill; Pillar capitals with lily work, chain-network and rows of pomegranates; A key figure is identified as the son of a widow; God fills craftsmen with a spirit of wisdom for sacred work; Two named bronze pillars, Jachin and Boaz, before the temple.

Only in David's mountains and mail; Solomon's wind, copper, jinn and staff: God made a spring of molten copper (or brass) flow for Solomon; The jinn did not know the unseen, else they would not have stayed in humiliating labor; Solomon dies leaning on his staff; only a creature of the earth gnawing the staff reveals his death when he falls; David and the coat of mail [contrast between the texts]; How Solomon died and how his death became known [divergence between the texts]; Rivers clap their hands and mountains sing together before YHWH; How Solomon's great bronze works were produced [divergence between the texts]; God taught David the craft of making coats of mail; The stormy wind is subjected to Solomon, blowing at his command; A great cast-bronze 'sea' basin rests on twelve bronze oxen facing the four directions in threes; Mountains and birds are made to glorify God together with David; Devils (shayāṭīn) and jinn labor for Solomon, diving and building; and 1 more.

title: The ark brought into the temple; the cloud fills the house ↔ Talut (Saul), the ark and Jalut (Goliath)
summary: 1 correspondence read side by side: 1 opposite ruling.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/01-hb-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: What the ark contains [contrast between the texts] (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in The ark brought into the temple; the cloud fills the house: Ark brought in procession into the temple at the autumn feast in the seventh month; Ends of the ark's poles visible from the holy place but not outside, 'to this day'; Sheep and cattle sacrificed so many that they could not be counted; Temple called a 'house of zebul' (exalted dwelling), a place for God to dwell forever; God has said he will dwell in thick darkness ('arafel); Archaic (Canaanite/Phoenician) month names Ziv, Bul and Ethanim are used; The tablets of the testimony are placed inside the ark; The cloud and glory fill the sanctuary so that even the leader cannot enter; Two golden cherubim face each other with wings spread over the ark.

Only in Talut (Saul), the ark and Jalut (Goliath): The ark (tabut) returns, carried by angels, containing tranquility (sakina) and relics left by the family of Moses and Aaron; David kills Jalut (Goliath) and is given kingship and wisdom; Were it not for God checking people by means of others, the earth would be corrupted; 'How many a small band has overcome a large one by God's leave'; God chose the king and increased him in knowledge and stature, though he lacked wealth; The people object that the chosen king has no wealth and they have more right to kingship; Before battle the army is tested at a river: whoever drinks is not with the leader, except a handful scooped by hand; The ark of the covenant: a gold-plated acacia chest with rings and poles [divergence between the texts]; David kills the Philistine giant [divergence between the texts]; A giant taunts Israel and is killed by a hero; A jar of manna preserved before the testimony for future generations; Objection raised against the newly chosen king [divergence between the texts]; and 10 more.

title: Solomon's prayer of dedication ↔ Solomon's blessing and dedication prayer on the bronze platform
summary: 7 shared motifs, found by the separate reads; not yet compared side by side.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: 'There is no man who does not sin' (weight 6.7); A foreigner from a far land who hears of God's name comes to pray at the temple and is heard (weight 6.7); Heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain God, much less a temple (weight 6.3); The direction faced in prayer [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.0); Prayers made toward the temple (or toward the land, city and house when in exile) are heard in heaven (weight 6.0); Prophet spreads out his palms to God in prayer (weight 5.4); Heaven and the heaven of heavens belong to God (weight 5.4). Pair score 42.5.

Only in Solomon's prayer of dedication: Exiles in an enemy land turn back with all their heart and pray toward their land, and God grants them mercy before captors; A man accused swears a curse-oath before the altar, and God judges guilty and innocent; Long catalogue of curses for covenant violation (disease, defeat, famine, exile); Egypt called an iron furnace (smelting furnace); Heaven is shut and no rain falls because of the people's sin; repentance brings rain; God alone knows the hearts of all humans.

Only in Solomon's blessing and dedication prayer on the bronze platform: Prayer lists famine, pestilence, blight, mildew, locust, siege and sickness as occasions for prayer; The king kneels on a bronze platform in the court and spreads his hands to heaven; An oath sworn before God's altar in the temple, judged by God; People away from Jerusalem or in exile pray in the direction of the land, city and temple; Captives confess in exile 'We have sinned, done wrong and acted wickedly'; 'Arise, YHWH, to your resting place, you and the ark of your might'; Temple called a 'house of zebul' (exalted dwelling), a place for God to dwell forever; 'O my servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of God's mercy; God forgives all sins'; God has said he will dwell in thick darkness ('arafel); The dynasty's continuance is conditioned on the heirs' faithfulness; God looks on the heart, not on appearance or height; Sacrifice only at the place God will choose to make his name dwell; and 1 more.

title: Nabal the fool, Abigail the wise and David's averted vengeance ↔ The disbelievers, the help, and the flame
summary: 1 correspondence read side by side: 1 same element.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/08-hb-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: A person's name declared to match his character: 'as his name is, so is he' (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Nabal the fool, Abigail the wise and David's averted vengeance: The soul bound in 'the bundle of the living' with God; A rich man insultingly refuses food to the hero's men at a feast; On hearing the news a man's heart dies within him and he becomes like stone, then dies; The hero marries the widow of a man who wronged him; An outlaw band claims a gift for having protected a rich man's shepherds; The king gives the hero's wife (his own daughter) to another man; God will make for the chosen one a 'sure house' (enduring dynasty); The hero adds wives to his household; Sheep-shearing as an occasion for travel and festivity; A wise woman intercepts an avenging warrior with gifts and speech and averts bloodshed; Every male cut off, idiom 'one who pisses against the wall', 'bond and free'; Host runs to welcome strangers, washes their feet and feeds them.

Only in The disbelievers, the help, and the flame: Curse on Abu Lahab ('father of flame'): his hands perish, he will burn in a fire of flame, and his wife carries firewood with a rope of palm fiber (masad) on her neck; Repeated mutual disavowal: 'I do not worship what you worship, nor do you worship what I worship'; 'to you your religion and to me mine'; Foreign daughter-in-law swears to follow her mother-in-law: your people my people, your God my God [contrast between the texts]; When God's help and the opening (al-fath) come, people enter God's religion in crowds; the prophet is to glorify and seek forgiveness; Wealth does not profit on the day of wrath.

title: Amalekites burn Ziklag; David recovers all and makes the spoil law ↔ Al-Fath: the clear opening, the sakina, the hand of God over their hands and the bedouin who stayed behind
summary: 1 correspondence read side by side: 1 opposite ruling.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/07-hb-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: Whether those who stayed behind share in the spoil [contrast between the texts] (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Amalekites burn Ziklag; David recovers all and makes the spoil law: A sick slave abandoned by the raiders is revived with food and guides the hero to them; The hero recovers every captive and all the spoil, nothing missing; The enemy is caught off guard while eating, drinking and celebrating their spoil; Part of the army is too exhausted to cross a stream and stays behind; Only four hundred young men escape on camels; Leader sends portions of spoil as gifts to the elders of many towns; People weep until they have no strength left to weep; Amalek attacks Israel on the way; Hero consults God through the ephod with yes/no questions about future events; Returning warriors divide the spoil with their brothers at home; The people are about to stone their leader.

title: Jehoshaphat's fast and prayer; the Levite oracle; enemies destroy one another as the choir sings ↔ Female deities, Satan's vow, slit cattle ears, and Abraham the friend
summary: 1 correspondence read side by side: 1 same element.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/02-hb-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: Abraham is called God's friend (ohev, 'lover') (weight 6.3). Pair score 6.3.

Only in Jehoshaphat's fast and prayer; the Levite oracle; enemies destroy one another as the choir sings: Prophetic assurance: 'the battle is not yours but God's'; The army arrives to find the enemy host all corpses on the ground, none escaped; 'Believe in YHWH and you will be established' (wordplay ha'aminu/te'amenu); A coalition of Moab, Ammon and their allies invades Judah from beyond the Dead Sea; Nations Israel was forbidden to attack during the exodus now repay this by attacking; The king stands in the temple court before the assembly and prays in a national crisis; 'We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you'; The king proclaims a fast throughout the land in a crisis; Ships built in alliance with a wicked king are wrecked, as a prophet foretold; Singers praising God march ahead of the army into battle; The spoil is so great that gathering it takes three days; The army returns in procession with harps, lyres and trumpets to the temple; and 9 more.

Only in Female deities, Satan's vow, slit cattle ears, and Abraham the friend: Satan commands people to alter God's creation; Idolaters invoke only female beings besides God, and only a rebellious Satan; Salvation is not by your wishes nor those of the People of the Book: whoever does evil is requited; Cursed Satan vows to take an appointed share (naṣīb mafrūḍ) of God's servants; Satan commands people to slit the ears of cattle (a pagan dedication rite); The faithless wife credits her lovers (the Baals) with her bread, water, wool, flax, oil and drink, not knowing God gave them; Offerings, incense and libations to the 'Queen of Heaven'; Whoever does good, male or female, and believes, enters paradise; God does not forgive associating partners with him (shirk) but forgives anything less; Not wronged by a date-stone's thread (fatīl) or groove (naqīr): proverbial minimal measures; Follow the religion (milla) of Abraham the ḥanīf, who was no idolater.

title: Jehoiada's coup with the Levites; Joash crowned, Athaliah killed, Baal temple destroyed ↔ Hunayn, the impurity of polytheists, the jizya
summary: 1 correspondence read side by side: 1 deliberately changed.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/03-hb-quran.yaml).

Shared motifs, rarest first: Gatekeepers stationed so that no one unclean enters the temple (weight 6.7); Those counted impure are kept out of the sanctuary [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7). Pair score 13.4.

Only in Jehoiada's coup with the Levites; Joash crowned, Athaliah killed, Baal temple destroyed: After the usurper's execution the people rejoice and the city is quiet; A priestly coup is timed to the Sabbath change of temple guards, keeping both shifts; The newly crowned king stands by his pillar at the entrance; The usurper is led out so that she is not killed in the house of YHWH; The usurping queen tears her clothes and cries 'Treason, treason!'; The temple of Baal is torn down and its priest slain before the altars; Coronation in which the king receives the crown (nezer) and the 'testimony' (edut); King David's spears and shields kept in the temple are issued to the guards; A priest organizes the guards to overthrow a ruler and enthrone the hidden heir; King and people enter a covenant to seek or serve YHWH in a public ceremony; People acclaim 'Long live the king!'; Chronicles differs in a specific detail from its parallel in Samuel–Kings.

Only in Hunayn, the impurity of polytheists, the jizya: People of the Book who do not follow the true religion are fought until they pay the jizya, subdued; Polytheists are impure (najas) and may not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year; No foreigner uncircumcised in heart and flesh may enter the sanctuary; A large army must not claim the victory for itself [divergence between the texts]; City accepting peace becomes forced labor; one resisting has its males killed; The believers' pride in their great numbers avails nothing and the earth grows narrow for them (Hunayn); God supports the prophet with hosts (junud) the believers did not see; God reinforces the believers in battle with a thousand (or more) angels; God sends down his sakina (tranquility, cf. shekhinah) on the prophet and believers.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A small enemy force defeats a very great army because the people forsook God (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Joash repairs the temple with the collection chest; after Jehoiada's death he stones Zechariah: A king who was righteous under a mentor turns to idolatry after the mentor's death; A child king does right as long as his priestly guardian lives; A chest is set at the temple gate for donations, emptied daily by royal and priestly officials; A murdered prophet's dying words call on God to see and avenge; A king kills the son of the man who saved and raised him, forgetting his loyalty; The Levites are slow to carry out the king's command and are rebuked; A priest is buried among the kings because of the good he did; The priestly guardian takes two wives for the king; The priest dies old and full of days at 130; A prophet is stoned in the temple court at the king's command; God sends prophets to warn the people but they will not listen; Surplus donations are made into gold and silver temple vessels; and 9 more.

matches.note: Who tests whom: in Chronicles the queen comes to test Solomon with riddles (lənassôt ʾet Šəlōmōh bə-ḥîdôt) and he answers all (wə-lōʾ neʿlam dāvār miš-Šəlōmōh); in the Quran Solomon tests the queen: nakkirū lahā ʿarshahā nanẓur a-tahtadī, and she answers ka-annahu huwa.

passages.text: וּמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א שָֽׁמְעָה֮ אֶת שֵׁ֣מַע שְׁלֹמֹה֒ וַתָּב֣וֹא לְנַסּוֹת֩ אֶת שְׁלֹמֹ֨ה בְחִיד֜וֹת בִּירֽוּשָׁלִַ֗ם בְּחַ֣יִל כָּבֵ֣ד מְאֹ֡ד וּ֠גְמַלִּים נֹשְׂאִ֨ים בְּשָׂמִ֧ים וְזָהָ֛ב לָרֹ֖ב וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה וַתָּבוֹא֙ אֶל שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה וַתְּדַבֵּ֣ר עִמּ֔וֹ אֵ֛ת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָיָ֖ה עִם לְבָבָֽהּ
וַיַּגֶּד לָ֥הּ שְׁלֹמֹ֖ה אֶת כָּל דְּבָרֶ֑יהָ וְלֹֽא נֶעְלַ֤ם דָּבָר֙ מִשְּׁלֹמֹ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֧ר לֹ֦א הִגִּ֖יד לָֽהּ
قَالَ نَكِّرُوا۟ لَهَا عَرْشَهَا نَنظُرْ أَتَهْتَدِىٓ أَمْ تَكُونُ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ لَا يَهْتَدُونَ
فَلَمَّا جَآءَتْ قِيلَ أَهَٰكَذَا عَرْشُكِ قَالَتْ كَأَنَّهُۥ هُوَ وَأُوتِينَا ٱلْعِلْمَ مِن قَبْلِهَا وَكُنَّا مُسْلِمِينَ

matches.label: The queen of Sheba's gifts and Solomon's response
matches.note: The gifts: Chronicles has the queen bring 120 talents of gold, spices and gems, which Solomon accepts, and he gives her all she desires (nātan ... ʾet kol ḥefṣāh). In the Quran she sends a gift (hadiyya) to test him, and Solomon refuses it, a-tumiddūnani bi-mālin fa-mā ātāniya llāhu khayrun mimmā ātākum, and threatens to invade with armies they cannot resist.

passages.text: וּמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א שָֽׁמְעָה֮ אֶת שֵׁ֣מַע שְׁלֹמֹה֒ וַתָּב֣וֹא לְנַסּוֹת֩ אֶת שְׁלֹמֹ֨ה בְחִיד֜וֹת בִּירֽוּשָׁלִַ֗ם בְּחַ֣יִל כָּבֵ֣ד מְאֹ֡ד וּ֠גְמַלִּים נֹשְׂאִ֨ים בְּשָׂמִ֧ים וְזָהָ֛ב לָרֹ֖ב וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה וַתָּבוֹא֙ אֶל שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה וַתְּדַבֵּ֣ר עִמּ֔וֹ אֵ֛ת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָיָ֖ה עִם לְבָבָֽהּ
וַתִּתֵּ֨ן לַמֶּ֜לֶךְ מֵאָ֥ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֣ים כִּכַּ֣ר זָהָ֗ב וּבְשָׂמִ֛ים לָרֹ֥ב מְאֹ֖ד וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה וְלֹ֤א הָיָה֙ כַּבֹּ֣שֶׂם הַה֔וּא אֲשֶׁר נָתְנָ֥ה מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֖א לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹֽה
וְהַמֶּ֨לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֜ה נָתַ֣ן לְמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א אֶת כָּל חֶפְצָהּ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁאָ֔לָה מִלְּבַ֖ד אֲשֶׁר הֵבִ֣יאָה אֶל הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַֽתַּהֲפֹ֛ךְ וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ לְאַרְצָ֖הּ הִ֥יא וַעֲבָדֶֽיהָ
وَإِنِّى مُرْسِلَةٌ إِلَيْهِم بِهَدِيَّةٍ فَنَاظِرَةٌۢ بِمَ يَرْجِعُ ٱلْمُرْسَلُونَ
فَلَمَّا جَآءَ سُلَيْمَٰنَ قَالَ أَتُمِدُّونَنِ بِمَالٍ فَمَآ ءَاتَىٰنِۦَ ٱللَّهُ خَيْرٌ مِّمَّآ ءَاتَىٰكُم بَلْ أَنتُم بِهَدِيَّتِكُمْ تَفْرَحُونَ
ٱرْجِعْ إِلَيْهِمْ فَلَنَأْتِيَنَّهُم بِجُنُودٍ لَّا قِبَلَ لَهُم بِهَا وَلَنُخْرِجَنَّهُم مِّنْهَآ أَذِلَّةً وَهُمْ صَٰغِرُونَ

matches.label: The queen of Sheba overwhelmed by Solomon's buildings
matches.note: The queen overwhelmed by Solomon's building: Chronicles has her see the house he built (wə-hab-bayit ʾăšer bānâ) until wə-lōʾ hāyâ ʿôd bāh rûaḥ; the Quran has the palace of smooth glass (ṣarḥun mumarradun min qawārīr) that she takes for deep water (ḥasibathu lujjatan) and uncovers her legs. Awe becomes a test she fails and then learns from. cf. Targum Sheni Esther 1:2 (glass floor), outside the HB.

passages.text: וַתֵּ֨רֶא֙ מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֔א אֵ֖ת חָכְמַ֣ת שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וְהַבַּ֖יִת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנָֽה
וּמַאֲכַ֣ל שֻׁלְחָנ֡וֹ וּמוֹשַׁ֣ב עֲבָדָיו֩ וּמַעֲמַ֨ד מְשָׁרְתָ֜יו וּמַלְבּֽוּשֵׁיהֶ֗ם וּמַשְׁקָיו֙ וּמַלְבּ֣וּשֵׁיהֶ֔ם וַעֲלִיָּת֔וֹ אֲשֶׁ֥ר יַעֲלֶ֖ה בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֑ה וְלֹא הָ֥יָה ע֛וֹד בָּ֖הּ רֽוּחַ

قِيلَ لَهَا ٱدْخُلِى ٱلصَّرْحَ فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهُ حَسِبَتْهُ لُجَّةً وَكَشَفَتْ عَن سَاقَيْهَا قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ صَرْحٌ مُّمَرَّدٌ مِّن قَوَارِيرَ قَالَتْ رَبِّ إِنِّى ظَلَمْتُ نَفْسِى وَأَسْلَمْتُ مَعَ سُلَيْمَٰنَ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ

matches.label: What the queen of Sheba says of Solomon's God
matches.note: The queen's last word: Chronicles has a blessing of Solomon's God, yəhî YHWH ʾĕlōhêkā bārûkh ʾăšer ḥāfēṣ bəkhā lə-tittəkhā ʿal kisʾô, 'your God', praised for Israel's king. The Quran has a conversion: rabbi innī ẓalamtu nafsī wa-aslamtu maʿa Sulaymāna lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn, after the hoopoe reported that she and her people worshipped the sun (27:24). Chronicles never calls her an idolater.

passages.text: יְהִ֨י יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֨יךָ֙ בָּר֔וּךְ אֲשֶׁ֣ר חָפֵ֣ץ בְּךָ֗ לְתִתְּךָ֤ עַל כִּסְאוֹ֙ לְמֶ֔לֶךְ לַיהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֶ֑יךָ בְּאַהֲבַ֨ת אֱלֹהֶ֤יךָ אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ לְהַעֲמִיד֣וֹ לְעוֹלָ֔ם וַיִּתֶּנְךָ֤ עֲלֵיהֶם֙ לְמֶ֔לֶךְ לַעֲשׂ֖וֹת מִשְׁפָּ֥ט וּצְדָקָֽה

matches.label: The great throne in the Sheba story, and whose it is
matches.note: The great throne: Chronicles praises Solomon's own (wa-yyaʿaś ham-melekh kissēʾ šēn gādôl wa-yṣappēhû zāhāv ṭāhôr); in the Quran the great throne is the queen's (wa-lahā ʿarshun ʿaẓīmun), and Solomon has it carried to him in the blink of an eye by one with knowledge of the Book.

passages.text: וַיַּ֧עַשׂ הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ כִּסֵּא שֵׁ֖ן גָּד֑וֹל וַיְצַפֵּ֖הוּ זָהָ֥ב טָהֽוֹר

matches.label: The queen of Sheba visits Solomon
matches.note: jiʾtuka min Sabaʾin bi-nabaʾin yaqīnin innī wajadtu mraʾatan tamlikuhum ~ û-malkat Šəvāʾ šāməʿâ ʾet šēmaʿ Šəlōmōh wat-tāvôʾ: a woman ruling Sheba (Sabaʾ / Šəvāʾ), a report (nabaʾ / šēmaʿ), and her coming to Solomon. The direction of the report is reversed: in Chronicles she hears of Solomon, in the Quran Solomon hears of her through the hoopoe.

title: Athaliah's usurpation and the hidden prince Joash ↔ Jehoiada's coup with the Levites; Joash crowned, Athaliah killed, Baal temple destroyed
summary: 5 shared motifs, found by the separate reads; not yet compared side by side.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: King David's spears and shields kept in the temple are issued to the guards (weight 6.7); Coronation in which the king receives the crown (nezer) and the 'testimony' (edut) (weight 6.7); A priest organizes the guards to overthrow a ruler and enthrone the hidden heir (weight 6.7); The temple of Baal is torn down and its priest slain before the altars (weight 6.7); People acclaim 'Long live the king!' (weight 5.8). Pair score 32.5.

Only in Athaliah's usurpation and the hidden prince Joash: Deposed ruler tears her/his garments crying 'Conspiracy, conspiracy!' or 'Treason!'; A condemned person is taken out so as not to be killed inside the sanctuary; A covenant is made between God, the king and the people; The king stands by (or on) the pillar in the temple according to custom; A queen mother seizes power by killing all the royal offspring; Sole surviving royal infant is stolen away with his nurse and hidden in the temple for years; Men tear their garments in grief or dismay.

Only in Jehoiada's coup with the Levites; Joash crowned, Athaliah killed, Baal temple destroyed: After the usurper's execution the people rejoice and the city is quiet; A priestly coup is timed to the Sabbath change of temple guards, keeping both shifts; The newly crowned king stands by his pillar at the entrance; The usurper is led out so that she is not killed in the house of YHWH; The usurping queen tears her clothes and cries 'Treason, treason!'; Gatekeepers stationed so that no one unclean enters the temple; Those counted impure are kept out of the sanctuary [divergence between the texts]; King and people enter a covenant to seek or serve YHWH in a public ceremony; Chronicles differs in a specific detail from its parallel in Samuel–Kings.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/03-hb-quran.yaml).

Only in Fall of Samaria and the sermon on Israel's exile: God warned the people by all his prophets and seers, 'Turn from your evil ways', but they would not listen; Vassal king withholds tribute and seeks help from Egypt, and is imprisoned; Kings or people practice divination (qesem) and augury (nihush); A capital city is besieged for three years before it falls; Theological sermon explaining the fall and exile of a nation as punishment for idolatry; Formula: he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat who made Israel sin; God calls Israel a stiff-necked people; King makes his son 'pass through the fire' after the abominations of the nations; Idols called 'elilim' ('nothings'); People bow down to all the host of heaven; An Assyrian king named in the narrative (Pul, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon); Conquered population deported to Assyria or another distant land; and 1 more.

Only in Israel asks for a god like the idol-worshipers: Israel asks its leader to make them a god [divergence between the texts]; People demand a king 'like all the nations'; Israel chosen as God's treasured people (am segullah) out of all peoples; Ruler orders the killing of male infants.

title: The resettled peoples, the lions and the syncretistic cult of Samaria ↔ Pagan portions and taboos; eight pairs; what is forbidden to all and to the Jews
summary: 1 correspondence read side by side: 1 same element.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/02-hb-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: Settlers fear YHWH yet serve their own gods (syncretism) (weight 6.7); Nations burn their sons and daughters in fire to their gods (weight 5.2). Pair score 11.9.

Only in The resettled peoples, the lions and the syncretistic cult of Samaria: Catalogue of foreign gods brought by settler peoples (Succoth-benoth, Nergal, Ashima, Nibhaz, Tartak, Adrammelech, Anammelech); Each land has a god whose 'manner' (mishpat) newcomers must learn; God sends lions to kill settlers who do not know the 'law of the god of the land'; Empire settles foreign peoples in the cities of a deported population; A deported priest is sent back to teach the settlers how to fear the local god; Mutual declaration: Israel avows YHWH as God, YHWH avows Israel as his treasured people.

Only in Pagan portions and taboos; eight pairs; what is forbidden to all and to the Jews: Pagans set apart cattle whose backs may not be ridden or burdened; Eight in pairs: sheep, goats, camels and cattle, male and female; which did God forbid?; Idolaters say 'had God willed we would not have associated partners nor forbidden anything'; Give its due on the day of harvest; For the Jews God forbade every animal with claws/undivided hoof and the fat of cattle and sheep except on backs, entrails or bone; Do not be wasteful; God does not love the wasteful (musrifīn); Pagans assign a portion of crops and cattle to God and a portion to their partners; Pagans declare certain cattle and crops taboo (ḥijr), to be eaten only by whom they will; Pagans reserve what is in the wombs of cattle for males, forbidden to wives unless stillborn; The camel is unclean because it does not have a split hoof [contrast between the texts]; List of clean and unclean animals: split hoof and chewing cud [response between the texts]; The fat tail of the sheep is offered [divergence between the texts]; and 11 more.

title: Hezekiah's reform; Sennacherib's invasion and the Rabshakeh's speech ↔ Sennacherib's invasion; the Rabshakeh's speech at the conduit
summary: 12 shared motifs, found by the separate reads; not yet compared side by side.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Officials ask the envoy to speak Aramaic, not Judean, so the people on the wall will not understand (weight 6.7); The people keep silent and do not answer the enemy at the king's command (weight 6.7); Enemy envoy addresses the besieged at the city wall to break their morale (weight 6.7); Invader promises deportees a land like their own, of grain, wine, oil and honey (weight 6.7); Each man under his own vine and fig tree, drinking from his own cistern (weight 6.7); Invader claims the defenders' own god sent him to destroy the land (weight 6.7); Egypt likened to a broken reed staff that pierces the hand of whoever leans on it (weight 6.3); Threat that the besieged will eat their own dung and drink their urine (weight 6.3); Taunt: Where are the gods of the conquered nations? Could they save their lands from my hand? (weight 5.8); An Assyrian king named in the narrative (Pul, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon) (weight 5.6); Command to smash altars, standing stones and Asherah poles and burn idols (weight 5.3); Men tear their garments in grief or dismay (weight 4.9). evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The king tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and goes into the temple in crisis (weight 6.7); The escaped remnant shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward; a remnant goes out from Zion (weight 6.7); The arrogant king boasts of climbing the heights of Lebanon and cutting its cedars, drying up rivers with his feet (weight 6.7); Sign: this year eat aftergrowth, next year what springs of itself, the third year sow and reap (weight 6.7); The 'virgin daughter of Zion' laughs at and wags her head after the enemy (weight 6.7); The enemy is said to reproach (harref) 'the living God' (weight 6.7); King spreads the enemy's threatening letter before God in the temple (weight 6.7); God says the conqueror's victories were planned by him long ago; the conqueror is only his instrument (weight 6.7); The angel of YHWH strikes 185,000 in the enemy camp in one night; at dawn all are corpses (weight 6.7); Royal parricides flee to the land of Ararat (weight 6.7); God puts a spirit in the invader so that he hears a rumor and returns home (weight 6.7); Proverb of crisis: children have come to the birth-stool and there is no strength to deliver (weight 6.7); God's angels strike the enemy army [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.3); Enemy king is murdered by his own sons while worshipping in his god's temple (weight 6.3); God defends the city for his own sake and for the sake of David his servant (weight 6.0); God will put his hook in the enemy king's nose and his bit in his lips and lead him back (weight 5.8); Conquered nations' gods were burned because they were no gods, only wood and stone made by hands (weight 5.8); Taunt: Where are the gods of the conquered nations? Could they save their lands from my hand? (weight 5.8); God addressed as enthroned (yoshev) on the cherubim (weight 5.4). Pair score 121.6.

Only in Hezekiah's prayer, Isaiah's oracle against Sennacherib and the angel's slaughter: God defends the city for his own sake and for the sake of David his servant [divergence between the texts]; When the punishment descends in their courtyard, evil will be the morning of those who were warned; Morning finds the destroyed lying prostrate (jathimin) in their dwellings.

Only in Hezekiah's prayer, Isaiah's oracle against Sennacherib and the angel's slaughter: The angel of YHWH strikes 185,000 in the enemy camp in one night; at dawn all are corpses [divergence between the texts]; 'The zeal of YHWH of hosts will accomplish this'; A remnant that survives judgment will be called holy and restored.

title: Elisha heals Jericho's water; the bears of Bethel ↔ The Companions of the Left in smoke and samum; who creates semen, crops, rain and fire?; the hidden Book; the soul at the throat

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/07-hb-quran.yaml).

Shared motifs, rarest first: God's power to make water sweet or bitter [contrast between the texts] (weight 6.3); Bitter water made drinkable by throwing in a piece of wood God shows the leader (weight 6.0). Pair score 12.3.

Only in Elisha heals Jericho's water; the bears of Bethel: Small boys jeer 'Go up, baldhead!'; the prophet curses them and two she-bears maul forty-two of them; Prophet throws salt from a new bowl into the spring and heals the deadly, miscarriage-causing water 'to this day'.

Only in The Companions of the Left in smoke and samum; who creates semen, crops, rain and fire?; the hidden Book; the soul at the throat: The damned eat of Zaqqum to fill their bellies and drink boiling water like thirst-crazed camels (al-him); A noble Quran in a hidden Book which none touch but the purified; The 'hospitality' (nuzul) of the deniers is boiling water and roasting in hell; The damned had lived in luxury and persisted in the great sin (al-hinth al-'azim); 'I swear by the positions (setting-places) of the stars, a mighty oath if you knew'; Have you seen the water you drink? Did you send it down from the rain-clouds? We could make it bitter (ujaj); For those brought near: rest (rawh), fragrance (rayhan) and a garden of bliss; The Companions of the Left are in scorching wind (samum), boiling water and the shade of black smoke (yahmum), neither cool nor kind; 'This is the certain truth' (haqq al-yaqin); Have you seen what you sow? Do you make it grow, or are we the grower? We could make it chaff; Fire kindled from a tree that God made grow [divergence between the texts]; The scripture exists with God in the 'Mother of the Book' (umm al-kitab), a heavenly archetype; and 7 more.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Dying man turns his face to the wall and prays, weeping (weight 6.7); A cake of figs laid on a boil heals the king (weight 6.7); Prophet tells the sick king 'Set your house in order, for you shall die' (weight 6.7); Given a choice of signs, the king picks the harder (shadow going backward) (weight 6.7); In answer to prayer God adds fifteen years to the king's life (weight 6.3); As a sign the shadow goes back ten steps on the stairway (dial) of Ahaz (weight 6.3); In answer to prayer God adds fifteen years to the king's life [contrast between the texts] (weight 6.3); At a leader's command the sun and moon stand still until the battle is won (weight 6.0). Pair score 51.6.

Only in Hezekiah's illness, the shadow on the steps and the Babylonian envoys: The king proudly shows foreign envoys all his treasures, prompting a prophecy of their loss; A king receives a foreign ruler's envoys and gift [contrast between the texts]; King accepts doom for his descendants, glad there will be peace and truth in his own days; Prophecy that the king's descendants will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon; King makes a pool and conduit to bring water into the city; God defends the city for his own sake and for the sake of David his servant.

Only in Hezekiah's illness, the shadow on the steps of Ahaz, and Hezekiah's psalm: Speaker laments that in the noon of his days he must go to the gates of Sheol, deprived of the rest of his years; A psalm-like 'writing' (mikhtav) of the king composed when he was sick and recovered; My dwelling is pulled up like a shepherd's tent; I have rolled up my life like a weaver, he cuts me off from the loom; In distress the sufferer chirps like a swift or crane and moans like a dove; God has cast all the speaker's sins behind his back and held back his soul from the pit of destruction; The dead cannot praise God: no wonders for the dead, no hesed in the grave, no faithfulness in Abaddon; A dying person's plea to God for more life, and God's answer [contrast between the texts]; On that day neither wealth nor sons avail, only one who comes to God with a sound heart; Bequest (wasiyya) to parents and kin prescribed for one who leaves wealth; altering it is a sin; Death or Sheol has gates (sha'arei mavet).

title: Hezekiah's illness, the shadow on the steps and the Babylonian envoys ↔ Solomon, the speech of birds, the ants, the hoopoe and the Queen of Sheba

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/05-hb-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: A king receives a foreign ruler's envoys and gift [contrast between the texts] (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Hezekiah's illness, the shadow on the steps and the Babylonian envoys: The king proudly shows foreign envoys all his treasures, prompting a prophecy of their loss; A cake of figs laid on a boil heals the king; Given a choice of signs, the king picks the harder (shadow going backward); Prophet tells the sick king 'Set your house in order, for you shall die'; King accepts doom for his descendants, glad there will be peace and truth in his own days; Dying man turns his face to the wall and prays, weeping; Prophecy that the king's descendants will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon; King makes a pool and conduit to bring water into the city; In answer to prayer God adds fifteen years to the king's life; In answer to prayer God adds fifteen years to the king's life [contrast between the texts]; As a sign the shadow goes back ten steps on the stairway (dial) of Ahaz; God defends the city for his own sake and for the sake of David his servant; and 1 more.

Only in Solomon, the speech of birds, the ants, the hoopoe and the Queen of Sheba: Entering Solomon's palace, the queen takes its floor of smooth glass for a pool and bares her legs; The hoopoe returns with sure news from Sabaʾ, knowledge Solomon lacked; Solomon sends the hoopoe to drop his letter before the queen and wait for their reply; Solomon reviews the birds, finds the hoopoe absent and threatens to punish or slaughter it unless it brings a clear excuse; An ʿifrīt of the jinn offers to bring the queen's throne before Solomon rises from his seat; Solomon's letter begins 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate' and demands submission; The queen sends a gift to see what the envoys bring back; Solomon rejects the wealth and threatens invasion; The queen confesses she wronged herself and submits with Solomon to God, Lord of the worlds; Solomon has the queen's throne disguised to test whether she recognizes it; she says 'It is as though it were it'; The queen and her people prostrate to the sun instead of God; Solomon inherits from David (knowledge and kingship); Solomon prays to be inspired to thank God for favor to him and his parents and to be admitted among the righteous; and 22 more.

title: Hezekiah's illness, the shadow on the steps and the Babylonian envoys ↔ Al-Munafiqun: false testimony, propped-up timbers, 'the mightier will expel the meaner', and the deathbed plea for delay
summary: 1 correspondence read side by side: 1 opposite ruling.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/08-hb-quran.yaml).

Shared motifs, rarest first: In answer to prayer God adds fifteen years to the king's life (weight 6.3); In answer to prayer God adds fifteen years to the king's life [contrast between the texts] (weight 6.3). Pair score 12.6.

Only in Hezekiah's illness, the shadow on the steps and the Babylonian envoys: The king proudly shows foreign envoys all his treasures, prompting a prophecy of their loss; A cake of figs laid on a boil heals the king; Given a choice of signs, the king picks the harder (shadow going backward); A king receives a foreign ruler's envoys and gift [contrast between the texts]; Prophet tells the sick king 'Set your house in order, for you shall die'; King accepts doom for his descendants, glad there will be peace and truth in his own days; Dying man turns his face to the wall and prays, weeping; Prophecy that the king's descendants will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon; King makes a pool and conduit to bring water into the city; As a sign the shadow goes back ten steps on the stairway (dial) of Ahaz; God defends the city for his own sake and for the sake of David his servant; At a leader's command the sun and moon stand still until the battle is won.

Only in Al-Munafiqun: false testimony, propped-up timbers, 'the mightier will expel the meaner', and the deathbed plea for delay: Spend before death comes and one says 'My Lord, if only you would delay me a little, I would give charity'; God delays no soul when its term comes; It is the same whether the prophet asks forgiveness for the hypocrites or not; God will not forgive them; The hypocrites testify 'You are God's messenger'; God knows he is, and testifies that the hypocrites are liars; The hypocrites say 'When we return to Medina the mightier will expel the meaner from it'; but might belongs to God, his messenger and the believers; Let not your wealth and children divert you from God's remembrance; The hypocrites' bodies impress and their speech is heard, but they are like propped-up timbers, thinking every cry is against them; The hypocrites take their oaths as a shield (junna) and will swear falsely even to God at the resurrection; When you eat and are full, beware lest you forget God; God forbids the prophet to pray or intercede for the people, for he will not hear; God sets a seal on the unbelievers' hearts and hearing and a covering over their eyes; God opens his good storehouse, the heavens, to give rain.

title: Josiah's temple repair, the finding of the book and Huldah's oracle ↔ Temple repair, finding of the book of the Torah, Huldah's oracle and covenant
summary: 5 shared motifs, found by the separate reads; not yet compared side by side.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Royal officials consult a woman prophet on behalf of the king (weight 6.7); A lost book of the law is found in the temple during repairs (weight 6.7); Because the king humbled himself, he will die in peace and not see the coming disaster (weight 6.7); Workmen handling sacred funds are not audited because they deal faithfully (weight 6.3); Men tear their garments in grief or dismay (weight 4.9). Pair score 31.3.

Only in Josiah's temple repair, the finding of the book and Huldah's oracle: A newly found sacred book is read aloud before the king, who tears his clothes; The king organizes the collection of silver for repairing the temple; A child of eight to twelve years becomes king.

Only in Temple repair, finding of the book of the Torah, Huldah's oracle and covenant: Prophet announces that the curses written in the found book will come upon the land; King stands at his place and makes the covenant before God; Levites skilled in music oversee the burden-bearers and workmen; The scribe reads the found book aloud before the king; Money collected by the Levites is given to the workmen to repair the temple; The book of the covenant is read aloud to the people; King and people enter a covenant to seek or serve YHWH in a public ceremony.

title: Josiah's covenant, purge of the cults and Passover; death at Megiddo ↔ The moving shadow, the night garment, the two seas and the constellations
summary: 1 shared motif, found by the separate reads; not yet compared side by side.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Worship of the constellations or zodiac signs (mazzalot) (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Josiah's covenant, purge of the cults and Passover; death at Megiddo: Idolatrous cult objects are burned and their dust carried away or thrown on graves; Despite the righteous king's reform, God does not turn from his anger over a predecessor's sins; Horses dedicated to the sun at the temple entrance and chariots of the sun burned; The high places Solomon built on the 'mount of destruction' (Mount of Olives) for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom; The righteous king is killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Necho; Priests of the high places are slaughtered on their own altars; An old prophecy (naming the future king) is fulfilled generations later; The bones of a prophet are left undisturbed when other graves are desecrated; Priests of the high places may not serve at the altar but eat unleavened bread among their brothers; The Tophet in the valley of Ben-hinnom is defiled so no one may burn children to Molech; A Passover such as had not been kept since the days of the judges; Women weave 'houses' (garments, hangings) for Asherah in the temple precinct; and 11 more.

Only in The moving shadow, the night garment, the two seas and the constellations: God extends the shadow, makes the sun its guide, then draws it back gently; God created humans from water and gave them kinship by blood and by marriage; Told to prostrate to the Merciful, the pagans ask 'What is al-Raḥmān?'; What God does after creating in six days [divergence between the texts]; God has inscribed a circle on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness; God made the night a garment, sleep a rest, and the day a rising (nushūr); As a sign the shadow goes back ten steps on the stairway (dial) of Ahaz; God set constellations (buruj) in the sky and adorned it for beholders; God the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting (al-hayy al-qayyum); God let loose the two seas, one sweet, one salt, with a barrier (barzakh) and partition between them; God makes winds his messengers (angels) and flaming fire his ministers; A solid firmament (raqia) separates upper waters from lower waters; and 6 more.

title: Jehoram's campaign against Mesha of Moab ↔ Al-Hashr: the first gathering and exile of the Banu Nadir, the cut palms, and the law of fay'
summary: 1 correspondence read side by side: 1 same element.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/07-hb-quran.yaml).
Shared motifs, rarest first: Do not cut down fruit trees during a siege: is the tree of the field a man? (weight 6.3). Pair score 6.3.

Only in Jehoram's campaign against Mesha of Moab: Besieged king offers his firstborn heir as a burnt offering on the city wall, and 'great wrath' falls on Israel, who withdraw; Prophet calls for a musician; as he plays, the hand of YHWH comes upon him; Prophet says he would not even look at the wicked king were it not for the righteous ally; Invaders fell every good tree, stop every spring and ruin every good field with stones; Allied kings on a seven-day detour run out of water for army and beasts and despair; A sheep-breeding vassal king pays tribute of a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams; At sunrise the water looks red as blood; the enemy thinks the kings have slain each other and rushes to plunder; Dry wadi fills with water though no wind or rain is seen; Standard regnal formula: age at accession, length of reign, mother's name, evaluation, burial, successor; Nations burn their sons and daughters in fire to their gods.

Only in Al-Hashr: the first gathering and exile of the Banu Nadir, the cut palms, and the law of fay': The expelled demolish their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers; Had God not decreed exile (jala') for them, he would have punished them in this world; God expelled the unbelieving People of the Book (the Banu Nadir) from their homes at 'the first gathering' (li-awwal al-hashr); Whatever palm trees (lina) you cut down or left standing on their roots was by God's leave; Later believers pray: forgive us and our brethren who preceded us in faith, and put no rancor in our hearts; Whether the enemy's trees may be cut down in a siege [contrast between the texts]; How spoil taken from the enemy is distributed [divergence between the texts]; Fay' (booty gained without cavalry or camels) goes to God, the messenger, kin, orphans, the poor and the wayfarer, so wealth does not circulate only among the rich; They thought their fortresses would protect them from God, but God came from where they did not expect and cast terror into their hearts; The poor emigrants and the hosts who prefer others over themselves even in need; whoever is saved from his own greed succeeds; Cities 'great and fortified up to heaven'; Spoils divided half to warriors, half to community, with a levy for God; and 2 more.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/04-hb-quran.yaml).

matches.note: Verdict, recognition and outcome. Sam: David burns with anger, ben-māweṯ hā-ʾîš, fourfold restitution; Nathan: ʾattâ hā-ʾîš; David: ḥāṭāʾṯî la-YHWH; pardon with a penalty, gam ha-bbēn ha-yyillôḏ ləḵā môṯ yāmûṯ, and the sword never leaves his house (12:10). Q: a calm verdict, la-qad ẓalamaka bi-suʾāli naʿjatika ilā niʿājihi; no 'you are the man'. David himself perceives (ẓanna Dāwūdu annamā fatannāhu) that it was a test, fa-staghfara rabbahu wa-kharra rākiʿan wa-anāb, and then fa-ghafarnā lahu dhālika wa-inna lahu ʿindanā la-zulfā wa-ḥusna maʾāb. Full forgiveness and honour, with no dead child and no curse on the house. The sin (Uriah, Bathsheba, 2 Sam 12:9) is never named.

evidence.text: Read side by side in both originals (alignments/hb-quran/06-hb-quran.yaml).

Shared motifs, rarest first: God strengthened David's kingdom and gave him wisdom and decisive judgment (fasl al-khitab) (weight 6.7); A prophet tells a case as if real; the king condemns the offender and is told 'You are the man' (weight 6.3). Pair score 13.0.

Only in The wise woman of Tekoa wins Absalom's return: A returned exile may not see the king's face; The king guesses who is behind a petitioner's speech; An only heir called 'my remaining ember' that kinsmen would quench; Mortality likened to water spilled on the ground that cannot be gathered up; A woman disguised as a long-mourning widow petitions the king with an invented case; Oath that not one hair of the person shall fall to the ground; A brother kills his brother in the first murder; A person praised as 'good (or wise) as an angel of God'; A wise woman intercepts an avenging warrior with gifts and speech and averts bloodshed; The 'redeemer of blood' (go'el ha-dam) kills the murderer.

Only in David's mountains, the two litigants and the ninety-nine ewes: Two litigants scale the wall of David's prayer-chamber (mihrab) and frighten him; A man with ninety-nine ewes demands his brother's single ewe and overpowers him in argument; A case about a ewe is brought to David for judgment [divergence between the texts]; 'O David, we made you a vicegerent (khalifa) on earth; judge between people with truth and do not follow desire'; David realizes he was being tested, asks forgiveness, falls down bowing and turns in repentance; David's repentance and what follows it [divergence between the texts]; A man with many sheep takes another's only ewe [divergence between the texts]; Shall God treat believers like those who spread corruption, the godfearing like the wicked?; The king confesses 'I have sinned' and the prophet announces forgiveness with a remaining penalty; Mountains and birds are made to glorify God together with David; God did not create the heavens and earth and what is between them in play (la'ibin) but in truth.

matches.note: wa-yyittənēm bêṯ-mišmereṯ ... wa-ʾălêhem lōʾ-ḇāʾ wa-ttihyênâ ṣərurôṯ ʿaḏ-yôm mutān ʾalmənûṯ ḥayyûṯ (shut up till death in a living widowhood) vs. wa-mā kāna lakum ... an tankiḥū azwājahu min baʿdihi abadā. The leader's women are withdrawn from any other man for life. In Samuel it follows Absalom's violation; in the Quran it is a permanent rule. The rabbinic ban on a king's widow remarrying is later (cf. only).

title: The last words of David ↔ The chain of revelation; Jesus, word and spirit; 'say not three'
